lead: Fuzzy clustering assigns every point a membership degree in every cluster, not one hard label. A point near a boundary can be 0.7 in one cluster and 0.3 in another. This is useful when groups overlap, as in medical image regions, customer segments, or noisy sensor readings. Only a few universities teach this advanced topic. The standard method is fuzzy c-means.
prereq: You need: hard k-means from Chapter 4.2, distance from Unit 1, and soft assignments from Chapter 4.4.

blocks.text: Hard k-means gives each point i one cluster label. Fuzzy clustering instead gives uik, the membership of point i in cluster k. Each uik lies in [0,1]. The membership matrix U has n rows and c columns.

For n points and c clusters, each point's memberships sum to one: Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>c</sup> u<sub>ik</sub> = 1. Here c is the number of clusters, and c<sub>k</sub> is centre k. The rule says a point has total belonging one, shared across clusters.
Membership is a weight, not a probability. It records overlap: a point at x=1 with centres 0 and 4 can be 0.90 in cluster 1 and 0.10 in cluster 2. Hard k-means would force 1 and 0.
Use fuzzy clustering when groups overlap, for example tissue regions in a scan, customer groups with mixed behaviour, or noisy sensor readings.
The fuzzy c-means objective is the weighted squared distance to every centre.
J = Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>c</sup> u<sub>ik</sub><sup>m</sup> d<sub>ik</sub><sup>2</sup>,  m > 1
blocks.where: J is the objective; u<sub>ik</sub> is membership; m is the fuzzifier; d<sub>ik</sub> is the distance from point x<sub>i</sub> to centre c<sub>k</sub>.

blocks.text: A larger m makes memberships softer. As m → 1, fuzzy c-means approaches hard k-means. As m grows, memberships move toward 1/c.
Alternating minimisation gives the update equations.

blocks.where: j runs over all clusters; d<sub>ik</sub> and d<sub>jk</sub> are distances from the same point i to centres k and j.

blocks.text: c<sub>k</sub> = Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> u<sub>ik</sub><sup>m</sup> x<sub>i</sub> / Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> u<sub>ik</sub><sup>m</sup>
blocks.where: x<sub>i</sub> is the data point; the denominator is the cluster's total fuzzy weight.

items: Initialise c centres, for example by random choice from the data.
Compute every distance d<sub>ik</sub> from point i to centre k.
Update all memberships u<sub>ik</sub> with the membership formula.
Update every centre c<sub>k</sub> with the centre formula.
Repeat until memberships or centres change less than a small threshold.

blocks.text: If a distance is zero, put that point fully in that cluster. Recompute distances after each centre update. Stop when memberships or centres change less than a small threshold.

figure.caption: The point x=1 is nearer to centre c1=0, so its membership in cluster 1 is 0.90 and in cluster 2 is 0.10.

spec.aria: Point x=1 is distance 1 from centre c1=0 and distance 3 from centre c2=4, giving fuzzy memberships 0.90 and 0.10.

examples.question: For point x=1, centres c1=0 and c2=4, and fuzzifier m=2, compute fuzzy memberships u1 and u2 using Euclidean distance.
examples.answer: The memberships are u1 = 0.90 and u2 = 0.10; they sum to 1.00.

traps: Memberships sum to 1 for each point; checking columns instead is a common mistake.
m must be greater than 1. m=1 is not fuzzy c-means in this form.
u<sub>ik</sub> is not a probability unless a probabilistic model is added.
The update divides by distance; if d<sub>ik</sub>=0, handle that point as full membership in cluster k.
A very large m can hide real cluster separation.

quiz.q: State the range of u<sub>ik</sub> and the sum rule for each point.
quiz.a: u<sub>ik</sub> ∈ [0,1]; Σ<sub>k</sub> u<sub>ik</sub> = 1 for each point i.

quiz.q: What values of fuzzifier m does fuzzy c-means require?
Why is fuzzy membership useful at a cluster boundary?
quiz.a: It records shared belonging, for example 0.6 and 0.4, instead of forcing one label.

quiz.q: For d1=2, d2=2, m=2, find u1 and u2.
For d1=1, d2=4, m=2, find u1 and u2.
Compare hard k-means labels with fuzzy c-means output.
quiz.a: Hard k-means gives one label per point; fuzzy c-means gives c memberships summing to one; hard is the limit m→1.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fuzzy c-means appears in medical image segmentation, remote-sensing maps, and soft customer segmentation. Toolboxes expose it as fuzzy c-means; search for "fuzzy c-means membership update" and "fuzzifier m". Research variants add noise handling, possibilistic memberships, and cluster validity indices. A useful next step is comparing fuzzy c-means with Gaussian mixtures on the same data.
